html:
The Fraser Canyon Gold Rush was the rush of some 30,000 miners, most of them from the California goldfields, to the lower Fraser River in what is now British Columbia in 1858.

Gold had been found on the Thompson and Fraser rivers, and when the Hudson's Bay Company sent some to the mint at San Francisco, the news set off the rush. Miners poured in through Victoria and up the river. Alarmed, Britain created the Colony of British Columbia that summer to keep control.

The diggings lay in the lands of the Nlaka'pamux, the St'at'imc and the Stó:lō, whose salmon fishing sites lined the canyon. Clashes led to the short Fraser Canyon War of August 1858, ended by a truce with Nlaka'pamux leaders near Lytton. A wagon road and trails were cut through valleys such as that of the In-SHUCK-ch. By 1860 most miners had moved on, many north to the Cariboo.
